summary:
Krasnoyarsk Krai stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation in full. The sources identify no deviation from that framework at the level of Krasnoyarsk Krai material enough to score separately, and the division is therefore assessed at the national score.

Under that framework, same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage is banned and gender transition is prohibited outright. Gender-marker changes on official documents are refused, legal gender recognition was banned in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute punishes public expression with administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. The expanded law reaches material that "justifies" gender transition. Since the 2023 Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation in it carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising carries 6 to 10 years.

Foreigners who violate these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers. The US State Department's advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and advises against all travel for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention, the war and arbitrary law enforcement alongside its warnings to LGBT travellers.

Enforcement is active and rising. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols, roughly 98 of them administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, that the state is able but unwilling to protect them, and it affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. The note also records the national position this division adopts: no regional deviation identified.
tangentialFactors:
The scale of enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over the preceding two years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where roughly 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, and a St Petersburg queer woman described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented in the wider national territory. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

These are national and neighbouring-region data points that frame what a visitor to Krasnoyarsk Krai can expect; they are not findings about venues or incidents inside the krai itself.
localsOnly:
The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025) sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims and affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. It finds that the state is able but unwilling to protect openly LGBT+ people, and that societal discrimination they face may amount to persecution.

The same note records that at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

Human Rights Watch's tally as of 30 June 2025 breaks down as roughly 98 administrative convictions and 3 criminal convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols since the 2023 designation; between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, with three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 exposed to up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people convicted across 98 administrative cases under article 20.3.

Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Krasnoyarsk Krai-specific enforcement data, arrest records, facility listings or document-office practices are sourced in this inventory; the division rests entirely on the national framework, and the absence of a recorded regional deviation is not the same as verified local non-enforcement.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian took place near Novosibirsk, outside Krasnoyarsk Krai, and is used here only as evidence of coercion documented in the wider national territory rather than as a finding about this division.

The Moscow bar raids, the St Petersburg interview and the pretrial death reported by the Associated Press are national-level incidents; whether equivalent raids or extremism charges have been brought inside Krasnoyarsk Krai is unresolved and not sourced.

The Meduza enforcement figures (eighteenfold growth, 60 million rubles in fines) and the HRW conviction tally are national aggregates with no breakdown by krai, so the local share of that enforcement volume remains not sourced.

The US State Department advisory gives no Russia-specific sub-national tiering for Krasnoyarsk Krai beyond the national Level 4 rating.
